idiom_name: package-level variable initialisers + func init() (both before main)
implementation_notes: Go has a real start-up phase: package-level variables are initialised in dependency order and init() functions run before main, sequentially in a single goroutine, so a package that opens its pool, pre-sizes its channels or pre-spawns its workers in init() has them ready for every caller. Keep failure handling explicit - init() cannot return an error, so anything that can fail in a recoverable way belongs in a NewServer()/Setup() called from main that returns an error, with panic reserved for state the process genuinely cannot run without. sync.Once is the lazy fallback when the acquisition may also be entered later, and sync.Pool is a different thing entirely: a cache of temporary objects, not an eagerly acquired resource.
pitfalls: init() cannot return an error: a recoverable failure either panics - aborting before main, with no graceful shutdown - or has to move into an explicit Setup() that main can handle.
Initialisation order is dependency-driven across packages and declaration-order within one package, so hidden ordering assumptions between init() functions break on refactoring.
Goroutines started in init() run concurrently with the rest of initialisation and must not assume the process is fully set up.
